lead: On the feast of St Thomas the Church reads two texts about foundations. Ephesians says that the household of God is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone”, and the Gospel shows one of those apostles at the moment his faith is laid. Thomas, who refused to believe a report, meets the risen Lord and speaks the highest confession in the Gospel of John: “My Lord and my God!” Psalm 117, with its refrain “Go out to all the world and tell the Good News” (Mark 16:15), turns the apostle’s faith into a mission to all nations. According to tradition, that mission carried Thomas as far as India.

r.h: Built upon the foundation of the apostles
set: Ephesians is a letter about the Church as one body of Jews and Gentiles in Christ. Just before our passage Paul, or the author writing in his name, reminds Gentile believers that they were once “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel” and “strangers to the covenants of promise” (2:12), and that in Christ the dividing wall has been broken down (2:14). They are now brought near, to share in what God gave to Israel.

Authorship. The letter claims to be Paul’s, written from prison (3:1; 4:1), and the Catholic tradition receives it as his. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul’s name soon after his death. In either case the Church reads it as Scripture. Some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus” in 1:1, which suggests that it may have been a circular letter for several churches.
str: v. 19: from outsiders to citizens: “no longer strangers and aliens”.
v. 20: the foundation: the apostles and prophets, and Christ as cornerstone.
vv. 21–22: the building grows into a holy temple, a dwelling for God in the Spirit.
kw: People living in a place without full rights. Paul says that the Gentile believers are no longer in that condition; they now belong to the household.
The stone at the corner that fixes the line of the walls. The image comes from Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22, which the New Testament applies to Christ (1 Peter 2:6–7; Mark 12:10).
The word naos means the sanctuary itself, where God dwells. The Church, built of living people, becomes his dwelling.
vv: you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God
Gentile believers are not guests in someone else’s home. They are members of God’s household, the same household that includes Abraham, Moses and the prophets.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.

The apostles are witnesses to the Resurrection, and their testimony is the foundation. Most scholars take “prophets” here to be the prophets of the New Testament Church (compare 3:5; 4:11); others include the prophets of Israel. The cornerstone, Christ, holds the whole together.
In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord
A living building: it “grows”. The Church is not finished, and each generation is another course of stones.
you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
“Together” and “spiritually”: the Spirit makes a community, not a collection of private believers, into God’s dwelling place.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it calls the Church God’s building: the Lord compared himself to the stone which the builders rejected, and on this foundation the Church is built by the apostles (CCC 756). The Church is also apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, in three ways: built on their witness, kept by the Holy Spirit in their teaching, and guided by their successors (CCC 857). Thomas, on this feast, stands for all the apostles whose faith became the foundation of the faith of others.

set: It is the evening of Easter Sunday, and the risen Jesus has appeared to the disciples behind locked doors, showed them his hands and side, breathed on them the Holy Spirit and given them power to forgive sins (20:19–23). Thomas, “one of the twelve”, was not there. John calls him Didymos, the Greek for “twin” (the Aramaic is te’oma). We have met him twice before in this Gospel: when Lazarus died he said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16), and at the Last Supper he asked, “How can we know the way?” (14:5).

Background. A week later, which is the Sunday after Easter, the disciples are again together. From earliest times the Church has seen in this the beginning of her gathering for the Lord’s Day. The passage is the last of John’s appearance stories; verses 30–31 that follow give the purpose of the whole Gospel: “that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God”.
str: vv. 24–25: Thomas is absent; he hears the news and refuses to believe on report.
v. 26: a week later Jesus comes through closed doors: “Peace be with you.”
v. 27: Jesus invites Thomas to touch his hands and side.
v. 29: the blessing on those who believe without seeing.
kw: Both the Aramaic name Thomas and the Greek Didymos mean “twin”. The Gospel does not tell us whose twin he was. Tradition gives him the name Judas Thomas.

The Greek says, literally, “do not become unbelieving but believing”. It is not a rebuke only; it is a call to become a believer. The verb “believe” in the Gospel’s purpose statement (20:31) comes from the same root.
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou

Kyrios, Lord, is the word used for the God of Israel in the Greek Old Testament, and theos is God. The Gospel which began with “the Word was God” (1:1) ends its stories with a disciple saying it of Jesus.
vv: Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.
Thomas wants no more than the others were given (20:20). He asks to see the Crucified. He is not the sceptic who asks for proof of just anything; he wants the wounds.
Although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
The same greeting as on Easter evening. The risen body is the same body that was crucified, and it is no longer bound by walls.
Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.

Jesus answers Thomas’ words one by one. He knows what Thomas said in his absence. John does not say that Thomas actually touched him; many early readers supposed he did, but the text shows him moved to confession at the sight of the Lord.
The highest confession in the Gospel, and Thomas is the one who says it. He does not say “you are like God”, but “my God”. The words are personal: my Lord, my God.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
The blessing looks beyond the apostles to every later believer. It does not scold Thomas for asking; it names the faith of all who rely on the apostles’ witness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the disciples’ doubt before the risen Jesus is part of the Gospel record: Thomas himself went through the test of doubt, so the idea that the Resurrection was a product of the apostles’ credulity is untenable (CCC 644). The risen body is the same body that was crucified, and it still bears the marks of the Passion, yet it already shares in the glory of God (CCC 645). St Augustine says that Thomas saw and touched the man and confessed the God whom he could neither see nor touch (in substance, Tractates on John 121). St Gregory the Great taught that the Lord allowed Thomas’ doubt so that the believers who came after him would be strengthened (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 26). Many Catholics say Thomas’ words silently as the Host and the chalice are raised at Mass.

qa: Thomas wanted to meet the risen Lord for himself, as the other apostles had (20:20). He was not condemned: Jesus came back for him a week later and spoke to him with gentleness. The title “Doubting Thomas” is too narrow. The Gospel shows him earlier as loyal to the point of death (11:16) and here as the one who makes the most complete confession of faith in the Gospel.
Did Thomas really come to India?

Thomas’ journey to India is not told in the New Testament. It rests on a strong and ancient tradition. The Christians of India have always held that he preached on the Malabar coast, and an early third-century non-canonical work, the Acts of Thomas, places him in India at the court of King Gondophares. Historians discuss the details, but the Church honours the tradition, and the Christians of India of several Churches honour him as the apostle who brought them the Gospel.
What does it mean that the Church is built on the apostles, if Christ is the cornerstone?

There is no rivalry. Christ is the cornerstone who holds everything together; the apostles are the foundation because they were chosen and sent by him, and they are witnesses of his Resurrection. Their authority is his, given to them (compare Matthew 28:18–20; CCC 857).
rite: St Thomas is listed among the Twelve in all the Gospels, and the Gospel of John gives him the most memorable lines. The feast was kept on 21 December in the Roman calendar until the reform of 1969, when it was moved to 3 July, the day on which, according to tradition, his relics were brought to Edessa (present-day Urfa in Turkey). Tradition also holds that Thomas reached the Malabar coast in the year 52, founded communities there, and was martyred at Mylapore, near present-day Chennai, about the year 72, where his tomb is venerated. For Catholics in India the feast is of special joy, and Christians of several Churches there honour him. His words, “My Lord and my God”, are among the shortest and fullest prayers of the Church.
study: Thomas asked to see the wounds of the Crucified. What in my own faith needs to meet the real Jesus, wounds and all, and not an idea of him?
Thomas was away when Jesus came. How can I make sure I am present when my community gathers on the Lord’s Day?
“Blessed are those who have not seen.” Who passed the faith to me, and how can I pass it on?
Ephesians says the Church is still growing. What small stone can I add to it this week?
